1.o: The inspired historian begins his narrative of the Acts of the Apostles, I. With a reference to, and a brief recapitulation of, his gospel, or history of the life of Christ, inscribing this, as he had done that, to his friend Theophilus, ver. 1, 2. II. With a summary of the proofs of Christ's resurrection, his conference with his disciples, and the instructions he gave them during the forty days, of his continuance on earth, ver. 3-5. III.
1.i: Acts 1 closes the Gospel story and opens the story of the church: Jesus leaves, and His friends are told to wait.
1.p: Lord Jesus, You ascended, and You will come again. While we wait, fill us with Your Spirit and make us Your witnesses. Amen.
1.l: Wait and pray today about something you cannot fix yet, and ask a friend to pray with you.
q: What is God asking you to wait for before you move?

2.o: Between the promise of the Messiah (even the latest of those promises) and his coming many ages intervened; but between the promise of the Spirit and his coming there were but a few days; and during those days the apostles, though they had received orders to preach the gospel to every creature, and to begin at Jerusalem, yet lay perfectly wind-bound, incognito—concealed, and not offering to preach.
2.i: On the day of Pentecost, the Holy Spirit comes on Jesus's followers, and about three thousand people believe.
2.p: Holy Spirit, fill us as You filled the first believers. Make us bold, loving, and generous. Amen.
2.l: Learn a few words in another language, and tell someone how God's Spirit brings people together.
q: The Spirit came on all the believers, not just a few. What does it mean that God's Spirit is for everyone?

3.o: In this chapter we have a miracle and a sermon: the miracle wrought to make way for the sermon, to confirm the doctrine that was to be preached, and to make way for it into the minds of the people; and then the sermon to explain the miracle, and to sow the ground which by it was broken up. I. The miracle was the healing of a man that was lame from his birth, with a word speaking (ver. 1-8), and the impression which this made upon the people, ver. 9-11. II.
3.s: Walking and Leaping and Praising God
3.i: Peter and John heal a man who had been lame from birth at the Beautiful Gate of the temple.
3.p: Lord Jesus, You give more than we ask. Heal what is broken in us, and let us praise You. Amen.
3.l: Give someone more than they asked for today, like your time, your attention, or a kind word.
q: The man asked for coins and got healing. What are you asking God for that He might want to give more of?

4.o: In going over the last two chapters, where we met with so many good things that the apostles did, I wondered what was become of the scribes and Pharisees, and chief priests, that they did not appear to contradict and oppose them, as they had used to treat Christ himself; surely they were so confounded at first with the pouring out of the Spirit that they were for a time struck dumb!
4.i: Acts 4 shows Peter and John, arrested for healing a man, answering the highest court in Israel with calm and courage.
4.p: Lord, give us boldness to speak of You, and courage to obey You above everyone else. Amen.
4.l: Tell someone today about something good you have seen God do.
q: They could not help speaking of what they had seen. What have you seen and heard that you've been holding in?

5.o: In this chapter we have, I. The sin and punishment of Ananias and Sapphira, who, for lying to the Holy Ghost, were struck dead at the word of Peter, ver. 1-11. II. The flourishing state of the church, in the power that went along with the preaching of the gospel, ver. 12-16. III. The imprisonment of the apostles, and their miraculous discharge out of prison, with fresh orders to go on to preach the gospel, which they did, to the great vexation of their persecutors, ver. 17-26. IV.
5.s: Out of Jail and Before the Council
5.i: Acts 5 starts with a lie and ends with a laugh, from the couple who deceived the church to apostles who walk out of jail.
5.p: Lord, give us courage to obey You rather than men, and joy in the cost. Amen.
5.l: Do the right thing today even if someone tells you not to, and do it with a cheerful heart.
q: Peter did not blame them for keeping some of the money, only for lying. Where is the lie in your giving, not the amount?

6.o: In this chapter we have, I. The discontent that was among the disciples about the distribution of the public charity, ver. 1. II. The election and ordination of seven men, who should take care of that matter, and ease the apostles of the burden, ver. 2-6. III. The increase of the church, by the addition of many to it, ver. 7. IV. A particular account of Stephen, one of the seven. 1. His great activity for Christ, ver. 8. 2.
6.s: Seven Men to Serve the Tables
6.i: The early church chooses seven men to care for the widows so the apostles can keep teaching and praying.
6.p: Lord, thank You for those who serve quietly. Help us to share the work and care for the overlooked. Amen.
6.l: Offer to help with a job at home or church today that no one wants to do, and do it cheerfully.
q: The apostles shared the work so everyone could do what they were good at. How do you share work with others?

7.o: When our Lord Jesus called his apostles out to be employed in services and sufferings for him, he told them that yet the last should be first, and the first last, which was remarkably fulfilled in St. Stephen and St. Paul, who were both of them late converts, in comparison of the apostles, and yet got the start of them both in services and sufferings; for God, in conferring honours and favours, often crosses hands.
7.i: Stephen is stoned for his faith, sees Jesus at God's right hand, and prays for those who kill him.
7.p: Lord Jesus, receive us when our time comes. Give us courage and love like Stephen's. Amen.
7.l: Forgive someone today who hurt you, and say it in your heart or out loud, the way Stephen did.
q: Stephen prayed for those who hurt him. How could you pray for someone who has wronged you?

8.o: In this chapter we have an account of the persecutions of the Christians, and the propagating of Christianity thereby. It was strange, but very true, that the disciples of Christ the more they were afflicted the more they multiplied. I. Here is the church suffering; upon the occasion of putting Stephen to death a very sharp storm arose, which forced many from Jerusalem, ver. 1-3. II. Here is the church spreading by the ministry of Philip and others that were dispersed upon that occasion. We have here, 1.
8.i: When persecution scattered Jesus' followers, Philip preached in Samaria, where many believed, and Simon the sorcerer was warned by Peter that God's gift cannot be bought.
8.p: Lord, You break down walls between people. Send us to share Your good news with those who are different from us. Amen.
8.l: Share some good news with someone different from you today: someone from another class, another place, or another group.
q: Philip crossed a wall of old hostility to share Christ. What wall might God be asking you to cross?

9.o: In this chapter we have, I. The famous story of St. Paul's conversion from being an outrageous persecutor of the gospel of Christ to be an illustrious professor and preacher of it. 1. How he was first awakened and wrought upon by an appearance of Christ himself to him as he was going upon an errand of persecution to Damascus: and what a condition he was in while he lay under the power of those convictions and terrors, ver. 1-9. 2. How he was baptized by Ananias, by immediate directions from heaven, ver. 10-19. 3.
9.s: A Light on the Road to Damascus
9.i: Jesus meets Saul, the persecutor, on the road to Damascus, and Saul becomes a follower of Jesus.
9.p: Lord Jesus, You changed Saul's life. Change ours too, and use us for Your purposes. Amen.
9.l: Pray today for someone who seems to be against God, and ask Him to change their heart.
q: Saul went from enemy to servant in one afternoon. Who in your life seems unreachable to you?

10.o: It is a turn very new and remarkable which the story of this chapter gives to the Acts of the apostles; hitherto, both at Jerusalem and every where else where the ministers of Christ came, they preached the gospel only to the Jews, or those Greeks that were circumcised and proselyted to the Jews' religion; but now, "Lo, we turn to the Gentiles;" and to them the door of faith is here opened: good news indeed to us sinners of the Gentiles.
10.i: Peter visits the Roman Cornelius, and the Holy Spirit falls on the first Gentiles to believe.
10.p: Lord, You show no favoritism. Help us to welcome everyone whom You welcome. Amen.
10.l: Welcome someone today who is different from you, and treat them as God does.
q: Peter had to learn that God accepts people from every nation. Whom are you tempted to leave out?

11.o: In this chapter we have, I. Peter's necessary vindication of what he did in receiving Cornelius and his friends into the church, from the censure he lay under for it among the brethren, and their acquiescence in it, ver. 1-18. II. The good success of the gospel at Antioch, and the parts adjacent, ver. 19-21. III.
11.s: The Disciples Were First Called Christians
11.i: In Antioch, Jews and Greeks follow Jesus together and are first called Christians, and the church sends out Barnabas and Saul.
11.p: Lord, You made one people from many. Send us out as Your witnesses. Amen.
11.l: Welcome someone who is different from you today and make a new friend.
q: Antioch's church was made up of Jews and Greeks together. Who are you learning to worship with that is different from you?

12.o: In this chapter we have the story, I. Of the martyrdom of James the apostle, and the imprisonment of Peter by Herod Agrippa, who now reigned as king in Judea, ver. 1-4. II. The miraculous deliverance of Peter out of prison by the ministry of an angel, in answer to the prayers of the church for him, ver. 6-19. III. The cutting off of Herod in the height of his pride by the stroke of an angel, the minister of God's justice (ver.
12.i: Herod arrests Peter, but the church prays, and an angel leads Peter out of prison.
12.p: Lord, You open prison doors. Help us to pray with faith, and to be glad when You answer. Amen.
12.l: Pray for someone in trouble today, and keep praying even when you wonder if it will work.
q: The church prayed for Peter and was surprised when he came to the door. Do you expect God to answer?

13.o: We have not yet met with any things concerning the spreading of the gospel to the Gentiles which bears any proportion to the largeness of that commission, "Go, and disciple all nations." The door was opened in the baptizing of Cornelius and his friends; but since then we had the gospel preached to the Jews only, ch. xi. 19. It should seem as if the light which began to shine upon the Gentile world had withdrawn itself.
13.s: The Disciples Were First Called Christians
13.i: In Antioch, Jews and Greeks follow Jesus together and are first called Christians, and the church sends out Barnabas and Saul.
13.p: Lord, You made one people from many. Send us out as Your witnesses. Amen.
13.l: Welcome someone who is different from you today and make a new friend.
q: Antioch's church was made up of Jews and Greeks together. Who are you learning to worship with that is different from you?

14.o: We have, in this chapter, a further account of the progress of the gospel, by the ministry of Paul and Barnabas among the Gentiles; it goes on conquering and to conquer, yet meeting with opposition, as before, among the unbelieving Jews. Here is, I. Their successful preaching of the gospel for some time at Iconium, and their being driven thence by the violence of their persecutors, both Jews and Gentiles, and forced into the neighbouring countries, ver. 1-7. II.
14.i: At Iconium, a crowd believes but the city divides, and Paul and Barnabas flee a plot to stone them.
14.p: Lord, give us boldness to speak and wisdom to know when to move on. Amen.
14.l: Keep doing what you know is right today, even when people don't like it.
q: The city of Iconium was split over the gospel. How do you act when people disagree about what you believe?

15.o: Hitherto we have, with a great deal of pleasure, attended the apostles in their glorious travels for the propagating of the gospel in foreign parts, have seen the bounds of the church enlarged by the accession both of Jews and Gentiles to it; and thanks be to that God who always caused them to triumph.
15.i: The apostles and elders meet at Jerusalem and decide that Gentiles do not need to follow the law of Moses to be saved.
15.p: Lord, Your grace is for everyone. Help us not to put heavy burdens on those who come to You. Amen.
15.l: Welcome someone who is different from you today, and don't ask them to be just like you.
q: The apostles listened to both sides before they decided. How do you listen when people disagree?

16.o: It is some rebuke to Barnabas that after he left Paul we hear no more of him, of what he did or suffered for Christ. But Paul, as he was recommended by the brethren to the grace of God, so his services for Christ after this are largely recorded; we are to attend him in this chapter from place to place, wherever he came doing good, either watering or planting, beginning new work or improving what was done. Here is, I. The beginning of his acquaintance with Timothy, and taking him to be his assistant, ver. 1-3. II.
16.i: At a riverside prayer meeting in Philippi, God opens the heart of a businesswoman named Lydia.
16.p: Lord, open our hearts to You, and open our homes to others. Amen.
16.l: Invite someone to your home or table this week, and make them feel welcome.
q: The Lord opened Lydia's heart. What do you ask God to open in you?

17.o: We have here a further account of the travels of Paul, and his services and sufferings for Christ. He was not like a candle upon a table, that gives light only to one room, but like the sun that goes its circuit to give light to many. He was called into Macedonia, a large kingdom, ch. xvi. 9. He began with Philippi, because it was the first city he came to; but he must not confine himself to this. We have him here, I. Preaching and persecuted at Thessalonica, another city of Macedonia, ver. 1-9. II.
17.i: Paul preaches in Thessalonica, a mob forms against his host Jason, and Paul is sent away by night.
17.p: Lord, You are the true King. Give us courage to follow You when it is costly. Amen.
17.l: Open your door to someone who needs a place today, even if it takes courage.
q: The crowd said Paul's message turned the world upside down. How could your faith do that?

18.o: In this chapter we have, I. Paul's coming to Corinth, his private converse with Aquila and Priscilla, and his public reasonings with the Jews, from whom, when they rejected him, he turned to the Gentiles, ver. 1-6. II. The great success of his ministry there, and the encouragement Christ gave him in a vision to continue his labours there, in hopes of further success, ver. 7-11. III.
18.s: A Year and a Half in Corinth
18.i: Paul works with Aquila and Priscilla in Corinth, preaches to Jews and Gentiles, and stays a year and a half.
18.p: Lord, You have people everywhere. Give us courage to keep speaking, and thank You for faithful friends. Amen.
18.l: Do your work today as if the Lord were your boss, and see how He might use it.
q: God told Paul he had many people in a city that looked tough. Where might God have people you have not met?

19.o: We left Paul in his circuit visiting the churches (ch. xviii. 23), but we have not forgotten, nor has he, the promise he made to his friends at Ephesus, to return to them, and make some stay there; now this chapter shows us his performance of that promise, his coming to Ephesus, and his continuance there two years; we are here told, I. How he laboured there in the word and doctrine, how he taught some weak believers that had gone no further than John's baptism (ver.
19.i: At Ephesus, God heals through Paul, a group of exorcists are humbled, and people burn their sorcery scrolls.
19.p: Lord, You are greater than every power. Give us courage to give up whatever holds us back. Amen.
19.l: Think of something you could give up today to follow Jesus more closely.
q: The Ephesians burned things worth years of wages to follow Jesus. What would it cost you?

20.o: In this chapter we have, I. Paul's travels up and down about Macedonia, Greece, and Asia, and his coming at length to Troas, ver. 1-6. II. A particular account of his spending one Lord's day at Troas, and his raising Eutychus to life there, ver. 7-12. III. His progress, or circuit, for the visiting of the churches he had planted, in his way towards Jerusalem, where he designed to be by the next feast of pentecost, ver. 13-16. IV.
20.i: Paul preaches until midnight in Troas, a young man falls from a window, and Paul brings him back to life.
20.p: Lord, You give life. Thank You for gathering Your people, and help us to stay awake to Your Word. Amen.
20.l: Listen carefully in church or at Bible time this week, and try not to fall asleep!
q: The church stayed up late to learn and share a meal. When do you make time for that?

21.o: We have, with a great deal of pleasure, attended the apostle in his travels throughout the Gentile nations to preach the gospel, and have seen a great harvest of souls gathered in to Christ; there we have seen likewise what persecutions he endured; yet still out of them all the Lord presently delivered him, 2 Tim. iii. 11.
21.i: A prophet ties himself up with Paul's belt to show that Paul will be arrested in Jerusalem, and Paul goes anyway.
21.p: Lord, give us courage to follow You when it is costly, and love for friends who do. Amen.
21.l: Pray for someone who is doing something brave today, and tell them you believe in them.
q: Paul's friends let him go, though it hurt them. When have you had to let someone follow God?

22.o: In the close of the foregoing chapter we had Paul bound, according to Agabus's prophecy of the hard usage he should receive from the Jews at Jerusalem, yet he had his tongue set at liberty, by the permission the chief captain gave him to speak for himself; and so intent he is upon using that liberty of speech which is allowed him, to the honour of Christ and the service of his interest, that he forgets the bonds he is in, makes no mention of them, but speaks of the great things Christ had done for him with as much…
22.i: Acts 22 gives Paul's own account of his life, told from the steps of a Roman fortress to a crowd that wanted him dead.
22.p: Lord, You turn enemies into messengers. Give us boldness to tell what You have done, and wisdom to know when to speak. Amen.
22.l: Tell someone your story today: what changed in your life, and who helped you.
q: Resisting one who spoke from heaven is dangerous. What have you been resisting that you already know came from him?

23.o: The close of the foregoing chapter left Paul in the high priest's court, into which the chief captain (whether to his advantage or no I know not) had removed his cause from the mob; and, if his enemies act there against him with less noise, yet it is with more subtlety. Now here we have, I. Paul's protestation of his own integrity, and of a civil respect to the high priest, however he had upon a sudden spoken warmly to him, and justly, ver. 1-5. II.
23.s: The Plot and the Young Man
23.i: A plot to ambush Paul is exposed by his young nephew, and a Roman escort takes him safely to Caesarea.
23.p: Lord, You keep Your promises, and You use people of every age. Make us brave like Paul's nephew. Amen.
23.l: If you hear that someone might be hurt, tell a trusted grown-up right away.
q: God used a young man to protect Paul. How could God use you to protect someone?

24.o: We left Paul a prisoner at Cæsarea, in Herod's judgment-hall, expecting his trial to come on quickly; for in the beginning of his imprisonment his affairs moved very quickly, but afterwards very slowly. In this chapter we have his arraignment and trial before Felix the governor at Cæsarea; here is, I. The appearing of the prosecutors against him, and the setting of the prisoner to the bar, ver. 1, 2. II.
24.i: Acts 24 is a trial with a polished lawyer, a calm prisoner, and a governor who almost listened.
24.p: Lord, give us courage to speak the truth to people in power, and to listen when You speak to us. Amen.
24.l: If you know you should do something good, do it today rather than waiting for a more convenient time.
q: Felix trembled and put it off. What conviction are you postponing until a more convenient time?

25.o: Some think that Felix was turned out, and Festus succeeded him, quickly after Paul's imprisonment, and that the two years mentioned in the close of the foregoing chapter are to be reckoned from the beginning of Nero's reign; but it seems more natural to compute them from Paul's being delivered into the hands of Felix. However, we have here much the same management of Paul's case as we had in the foregoing chapter; cognizance is here taken of it, I. By Festus the governor; it is brought before him by the Jews, ver.
25.i: Acts 25 is a chapter of delays and decisions, with a new governor, a hidden plot, and a prisoner who uses his rights as a Roman.
25.p: Lord, You guard Your servants in ways they cannot see. Give us wisdom as well as courage, and use our plans for Your purposes. Amen.
25.l: Be wise as well as brave today: pick the right moment and the right way to stand up for what is right.
q: Wisdom as well as patience is tested in hard times. Where do you need to be as wise as a serpent right now?

26.o: We left Paul at the bar, and Festus, and Agrippa, and Bernice, and all the great men of the city of Cæsarea, upon the bench, or about it, waiting to hear what he had to say for himself. Now in this chapter we have, I. The account he gives of himself, in answer to the calumnies of the Jews. And in this, 1. His humble address to king Agrippa, and the compliment he passed upon him, ver. 1-3. 2.
26.i: Paul tells King Agrippa his story and ends with a wish that everyone listening would believe.
26.p: Lord, we pray for those who are close to believing. Give us the kindness and the courage to share our story. Amen.
26.l: Tell someone one thing you believe about Jesus, and tell it kindly.
q: Agrippa was close to believing. What keeps people near, but not all the way in?

27.o: This whole chapter is taken up with an account of Paul's voyage towards Rome, when he was sent thither a prisoner by Festus the governor, upon his appeal to Cæsar. I. The beginning of the voyage was well enough, it was calm and prosperous, ver. 1-8. II. Paul gave them notice of a storm coming, but could not prevail with them to lie by, ver. 9-11. III.
27.i: A terrible storm drives Paul's ship for two weeks, and Paul promises that all on board will survive.
27.p: Lord, You are with us in every storm. Help us to trust Your word and to encourage others. Amen.
27.l: When you feel afraid today, say out loud, I believe God, and then take one small step.
q: Paul was a prisoner, yet he was the one who gave courage. Where can you give courage to others?

28.o: We are the more concerned to take notice of and to improve what is here recorded concerning blessed Paul because, after the story of this chapter, we hear no more of him in the sacred history, though we have a great deal of him yet before us in his epistles. We have attended him through several chapters from one judgment-seat to another, and could at last have taken leave of him with the more pleasure if we had left him at liberty; but in this chapter we are to condole with him, and yet congratulate him. I.
28.i: After the shipwreck, the people of Malta welcome the survivors, a snake bites Paul, and Paul heals the governor's father.
28.p: Lord, thank You for the kindness of strangers. Make us kind to everyone in need. Amen.
28.l: Be like the people of Malta today: help a stranger who is cold or lost.
q: The islanders showed kindness to strangers in need. How can you do the same?
